tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The notebook defines a train/validation split using RandomSplitter on the training CSV and performs model selection and hyperparameter experiments using the validation set. The competition test set (test.csv) is read only at the end to produce a submission and is not used for training or hyperparameter tuning.
EVIDENCE:
- Train data is loaded from the training CSV only: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb, cell  (code)  "df = pd.read_csv(path/'train.csv')"] (see cell  (code) displayed by the notebook).  (Cell index  where this appears: cell 12 in the parsed cells output above; shown in earlier inspection.)
- Train/validation splitting uses RandomSplitter on the training dataframe and the resulting indices are applied to create trn_indep/val_indep and trn_dep/val_dep: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb: cell 76 (code) "from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter\ntrn_split, val_split = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)"; cell 81 (code) where the code applies the indices to produce trn_indep, val_indep, trn_dep, val_dep].
  - Cell 76 (code): from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter; trn_split, val_split = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)
  - Cell 81 (code): trn_indep = t_indep[trn_split]; val_indep = t_indep[val_split]; trn_dep = t_dep[trn_split]; val_dep = t_dep[val_split]; ...
- Validation accuracy is computed explicitly using the held-out validation set: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb: cell 94 (code) "preds = calc_preds(coeffs, val_indep)"; cell 96 (code) "results = val_dep.bool()==my_preds"; cell 98 (code) "results.float().mean()"]. These cells show validation metrics are computed from val_indep/val_dep.
- Hyperparameter/learning-rate experiments are run by re-calling train_model with different lr values (e.g., cell 89 code: coeffs = train_model(18, lr=0.2); other calls to train_model(lr=1.4), train_model(lr=20) appear elsewhere). The notebook then inspects validation performance (as shown in the validation cells above), i.e., model selection uses the validation set rather than test set.
- The test set is read only at the end for submission and preprocessed after training: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb: cell 119 (code) "tst_df = pd.read_csv(path/'test.csv')"; cell 123 (code) shows preprocessing of tst_df and creation of tst_indep; cell 125 (code) "tst_df['Survived'] = (calc_preds(tst_indep, coeffs)>0.5).int()" shows predictions on test set are made only after training].

All of the above are directly visible in the notebook source at /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb (the relevant cells and code fragments were inspected and quoted). There is no code that reads test.csv earlier or uses the test set for model training or hyperparameter selection.

Therefore the repository passes the test: there is no leakage from test to train/validation, and any model selection/hyperparameter tuning is done using the validation set only.

If you want, I can also extract and paste the exact notebook cell contents for the cited cells into separate artifact files under /evidence/artifacts/ for easier verification.

REASON: The notebook performs a stochastic augmentation step by creating augmented_df and concatenating it into df (the dataframe read from train.csv) before the train/validation split. The code then uses RandomSplitter on df and constructs t_indep from df, so augmented rows are present in the dataset that is split into training and validation — therefore augmentation can affect the validation set. The test set (tst_df) is preprocessed deterministically and does not receive augmentation, so only the validation split is impacted.
EVIDENCE: 
- Augmentation applied to the main training dataframe: [/evidence/artifacts/augmentation_snippet.txt:1-1] shows the augmentation code that copies df, perturbs Age, and concatenates the augmented rows back into df.
- The train/validation split is produced from df: [/evidence/artifacts/trn_split_snippet.txt:1-4] shows RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df) producing trn_split and val_split, and the subsequent code uses these indices to create trn_indep/val_indep from t_indep.
- Independent-variable tensor is built from df (therefore includes augmentation): [/evidence/artifacts/t_indep_snippet.txt:1-3] shows t_indep = tensor(df[indep_cols].values, dtype=torch.float), demonstrating t_indep is derived from df that was concatenated with augmented rows.

These three pieces of code together prove that augmentation was applied to df prior to splitting, so validation data can include augmented examples — violating the requirement that augmentations are only applied to training data.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository uses PyTorch matrix and broadcasting operations for all per-row/per-element computations that would otherwise be implemented with explicit Python loops. The code computes predictions with vectorized operations (broadcasting and matrix multiply), and neural-net forward passes use matrix products. Remaining Python loops only iterate over small lists of parameter tensors (layers/consts) to update parameters or apply activations across layers — these are not per-element loops that should be replaced by matrix operations.
EVIDENCE: 
- Vectorized column-wise normalization using broadcasting: [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:269-270] shows vals,indices = t_indep.max(dim=0) followed by t_indep = t_indep / vals which divides the matrix by a vector via broadcasting.
- Initial vectorized prediction (elementwise multiply + row-sum): [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:292,319-321] shows preds = (t_indep*coeffs).sum(axis=1) and the calc_preds function using that form — no Python loops over rows.
- Replacement with explicit matrix product for efficiency: [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:727-738] demonstrates using val_indep@coeffs and then redefining calc_preds to return torch.sigmoid(indeps@coeffs), a matrix-vector product.
- Neural network forward passes use matrix-matrix products (no per-element Python loops): [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:800-804] (indeps@l1 and res@l2) and the deep network loop also uses res = res@l + consts[i] for each layer [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:874-878]. These loops iterate over layers (small lists), not over data rows.
- Parameter updates iterate over parameter tensors (not per-element): [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:812-816] and [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:855-857] show loops that call in-place tensor updates and .grad.zero_() on each parameter tensor.

Taken together, the code applies vectorized matrix operations and broadcasting for the heavy data computations (predictions, normalization, neural network layers). There are no explicit Python loops implementing elementwise or per-row arithmetic where equivalent matrix operations were available and unused. Therefore the test PASSes.

metadata.test_description: Code does not use explicit loops or Python control flow when matrix operations could have been used to implement the exact same operation more efficiently. If this property is not satisfied, show the matrix operations which should replace the raw Python logic.
metadata.reason_text: The repository uses PyTorch matrix and broadcasting operations for all per-row/per-element computations that would otherwise be implemented with explicit Python loops. The code computes predictions with vectorized operations (broadcasting and matrix multiply), and neural-net forward passes use matrix products. Remaining Python loops only iterate over small lists of parameter tensors (layers/consts) to update parameters or apply activations across layers — these are not per-element loops that should be replaced by matrix operations.
metadata.evidence_text:
- Vectorized column-wise normalization using broadcasting: [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:269-270] shows vals,indices = t_indep.max(dim=0) followed by t_indep = t_indep / vals which divides the matrix by a vector via broadcasting.
- Initial vectorized prediction (elementwise multiply + row-sum): [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:292,319-321] shows preds = (t_indep*coeffs).sum(axis=1) and the calc_preds function using that form — no Python loops over rows.
- Replacement with explicit matrix product for efficiency: [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:727-738] demonstrates using val_indep@coeffs and then redefining calc_preds to return torch.sigmoid(indeps@coeffs), a matrix-vector product.
- Neural network forward passes use matrix-matrix products (no per-element Python loops): [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:800-804] (indeps@l1 and res@l2) and the deep network loop also uses res = res@l + consts[i] for each layer [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:874-878]. These loops iterate over layers (small lists), not over data rows.
- Parameter updates iterate over parameter tensors (not per-element): [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:812-816] and [/kaggle/repo/converted_notebook.py.py:855-857] show loops that call in-place tensor updates and .grad.zero_() on each parameter tensor.

Taken together, the code applies vectorized matrix operations and broadcasting for the heavy data computations (predictions, normalization, neural network layers). There are no explicit Python loops implementing elementwise or per-row arithmetic where equivalent matrix operations were available and unused. Therefore the test PASSes.

  - [/evidence/artifacts/extracted.py:243] val_indep@coeffs
  - [/evidence/artifacts/extracted.py:245-246] calc_preds using indeps@coeffs
- Multi-layer network: loops over layers appear only to apply successive matrix multiplies + nonlinearities (not per-sample Python loops) — these are present at [/evidence/artifacts/extracted.py:294-302] where each layer is applied by res = res @ l + consts[i] and then a ReLU.   - [/evidence/artifacts/extracted.py:304-308] update_coeffs for multi-layer model

REASON: The repository does not contain the code artifacts needed to determine whether any data augmentation is applied only to the training dataset while validation/test use deterministic preprocessing. The repo contains a single Jupyter notebook (a Titanic tabular-data example) and metadata; there are no dataset/Dataset classes, no data loader or training scripts, and no image/audio augmentation or transform pipelines to inspect. Without the relevant code (data pipeline, transforms, or training/validation/test dataloader definitions), the property cannot be verified or refuted.

EVIDENCE:
- Repository top-level listing shows only two files: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb] and [/kaggle/repo/kernel-metadata.json]. (See listing in repository root.)
- The notebook contains tabular data preprocessing and training code for the Titanic dataset; it does not define image/audio augmentation or dataset split transform pipelines. Example excerpt showing the notebook content and that it reads CSV and uses pandas/pytorch for a tabular task: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1-60].
- Kernel metadata indicates the notebook is a Kaggle Titanic kernel and the code file is the notebook: [/kaggle/repo/kernel-metadata.json:1-19].
- A recursive keyword search for typical augmentation/transform/dataloader terms only matches the notebook file (i.e., there are no separate modules defining transforms or Dataset classes to inspect). The repository lacks files like train.py, data/*.py, datasets/*.py, transforms.py, or any image-augmentation libraries usage (torchvision/albumentations) that would be needed to assess the property.

What is needed to reach a non-inconclusive verdict:
- Provide the code that defines the data pipeline: Dataset classes, DataLoader creation, or training/validation/test split code and the transforms/augmentation pipelines (for example, files such as data.py, datasets.py, train.py, train_loop.py, or any scripts that set up torchvision.transforms or albumentations). Specifically, to verify the property I need to see either:
  - Separate transform/augmentation objects for training and validation/test and the code where they are applied (e.g., in Dataset.__init__ or in DataLoader creation), or
  - A training script showing that augmentations are only attached to the training dataloader and deterministic preprocessing is used for validation/test, or
  - A config file that unambiguously maps augmentations only to the training split.

If you can provide those files (or point me to the path in the repository that contains the data pipeline), I will re-evaluate and produce a PASS or FAIL with precise citations to the lines demonstrating the behavior.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository contains direct evidence that the test set is read and its values are used to compute scaling factors applied to the training data (data leakage). This means information from the test set influences training/validation. Therefore the property "No leakage from test to train/val sets" is violated.
EVIDENCE: The notebook reads the competition test.csv into a variable named tst_df_leak and constructs tst_indep_leak, then concatenates it with t_indep and computes the column-wise max (used to scale t_indep). See these lines in the notebook file:
- Test file read and preprocessing + concatenation and max (leak): [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:552-561]
  - Lines show: "tst_df_leak = pd.read_csv(path/'test.csv')", "tst_df_leak.fillna(modes, inplace=True)", "tst_df_leak['LogFare'] = np.log(tst_df_leak['Fare']+1)", "tst_df_leak = pd.get_dummies(...)", "tst_indep_leak = tensor(...)", "vals,indices = torch.cat([t_indep, tst_indep_leak]).max(dim=0)", "t_indep = t_indep / vals"
- The notebook also shows that a validation split is created using RandomSplitter (so there is a held-out validation set), but that does not prevent the leakage because scaling used the test set values. See split creation and application: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:827-834] and [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:903-910]

These lines provide direct, verifiable evidence that the test set is used to compute preprocessing (scaling) applied to training/validation data, which is data leakage and violates the test requirement.

If you would like, I can point to the exact JSON cell objects or create a small extracted snippet file under /evidence/artifacts/ showing the offending lines for easier review.

If you provide the requested run logs or saved result files, I will re-evaluate and then return PASS if the validation accuracy with randomized labels is near the random-guess baseline, or FAIL if it is not. Whether the training dataset order is shuffled (and whether the validation/test sets are left unshuffled) depends on the behavior of RandomSplitter (i.e., whether it returns indices in random order or in sorted order) — that behavior is part of the fastai library and is not present in this repository. Therefore, from the repository contents alone we cannot conclusively determine whether the training data is shuffled while val/test are not.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The code explicitly moves the model parameters (coeffs) to CUDA while the input tensors remain on CPU, producing inconsistent device placement and therefore either implicit CPU<->GPU transfers or runtime errors when arithmetic is attempted. Additionally, dtypes are not applied consistently: independent variables are created as float tensors but the dependent (target) tensor is created without a float dtype (likely torch.int64), so there's no consistent floating-point dtype policy (e.g., fp32 or bf16) across model, inputs and targets.
EVIDENCE: 
- Creation of dependent (target) tensor without explicit float dtype: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:434-437] ("t_dep = tensor(df.Survived)").
- Creation of independent variables as float tensors: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:458-461] ("t_indep = tensor(df[indep_cols].values, dtype=torch.float)").
- Training split assigns CPU tensors to training variables: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:903-909] ("trn_indep = t_indep[trn_split]... trn_dep = t_dep[trn_split]").
- The training loop uses coeffs together with the training tensors: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:948-949] ("loss = calc_loss(coeffs, trn_indep, trn_dep)").
- Initialization of coefficients moves them to CUDA: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:964-967] ("return (torch.rand(n_coeff)-0.5).requires_grad_().cuda()").

These lines together show coeffs are on GPU while inputs/targets remain on CPU and targets use a different dtype, directly refuting the test requirement for consistent single-device placement and consistent dtype policy.

There is no code that uses the test labels to tune or select models.
metadata.evidence_text:
- The training/validation split is created from the training DataFrame (df) using fastai's RandomSplitter: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1077-1078] and those indices are applied to create trn_indep/val_indep and trn_dep/val_dep [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1168-1173].

- The test set is read only after training and is preprocessed using statistics computed from the training data (modes and vals). The notebook reads the test CSV: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1641] and fills missing values using modes computed earlier from the training data [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1691]. The test features are normalized using vals computed from the (training) independent tensor [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:719-720 and 1695-1696].

- Evidence that preprocessing/statistics are computed from training data: modes are computed from df earlier in the notebook [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:194-199], and the per-column max values (vals) used for normalization are computed from the training independent tensor t_indep [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:719-720].

Note about other leakage: The notebook intentionally performs a simple augmentation step before splitting (duplicating df with small noise) which the author even comments "can leak into val/test"; see the augmentation code applied to df before the RandomSplitter [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:501-506]. This is leakage between augmented rows and the validation set (i.e., within the training data), but it is not leakage from the competition test set into training/validation nor is the test set used for model selection.

Given the above direct evidence, the repository satisfies the test criterion that there is no leakage from the test set into training/validation and no use of the test set for model selection/hyperparameter tuning.

REASON: The notebook implements model training using PyTorch tensors and manually updates all trainable parameter tensors. All parameter tensors are created with requires_grad_() and the training update functions iterate over every parameter tensor to apply gradient updates (no layers are left out). The only place where requires_grad is set to False is in a display helper called after training; it does not freeze parameters during training and training routines reinitialize parameters with requires_grad_() when needed.
EVIDENCE: 
- Parameters are created with gradients enabled:
  - Linear model init: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1240-1244] shows init_coeffs returning (torch.rand(...)).requires_grad_()
  - Neural net init (two-layer): [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:2021-2027] shows layer tensors returned with .requires_grad_()
  - Deep net init: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:2200-2203] shows for l in layers+consts: l.requires_grad_()

- Training loop updates all parameter tensors:
  - The generic update function for multiple coeffs iterates over layers and consts and updates each: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:2040-2046] and [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:2216-2226] (the update_coeffs implementations) perform layer.sub_(layer.grad * lr) and layer.grad.zero_() for each layer.
  - The one_epoch/train_model flow calls loss.backward() then update_coeffs under torch.no_grad(): [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1219-1224] and [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1253-1256].

- The only explicit disabling of gradients is in a display helper used after training:
  - show_coeffs sets requires_grad_(False) on coeffs for display: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1325-1327]. This call appears after the first training run and is used only for showing values; subsequent training calls reinitialize coeffs with .requires_grad_(), so parameters are not frozen during training (see re-initialization at [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1240-1244] and other init points).

Conclusion: All model parameters that are meant to be trained are created with gradients enabled and are explicitly updated by the training code; there are no frozen layers left out of the optimizer/update steps during training. Therefore the test PASSES.

VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The repository contains a Jupyter notebook that defines the dataset split and an accuracy function, but there is no code or documented experiment that randomizes the labels (dependent variable) and measures the resulting validation accuracy. Therefore I cannot determine from the repository alone whether randomizing labels causes accuracy to drop to the random-guessing baseline.

EVIDENCE:
- The notebook creates the dependent-label tensor from the Survived column: [cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:556-568]. This shows where labels are read into t_dep.
- The notebook splits data into training and validation and assigns val_dep = t_dep[val_split]: [cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1148-1172]. This shows the validation labels used for evaluation.
- The notebook defines an accuracy function that computes accuracy on val_dep: [cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:1438-1443]. This is the metric used for evaluation.
- The notebook applies random noise augmentation to input features (Age and LogFare), demonstrating randomness applied to features, not labels: [cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:499-506].

No code that randomizes/permutates labels was found in the repository (no occurrences of operations such as np.random.permutation applied to t_dep, or reassignments of t_dep with shuffled values). To conclusively PASS or FAIL the test, one of the following is required:

1) A code cell or script in the repository that (a) randomizes the training labels (for example by permuting t_dep for the training indices), (b) retrains the model, and (c) reports validation accuracy — then I could inspect those outputs in the repo to decide PASS/FAIL. If such a cell exists but is in hidden output only, include the executed notebook output or add a new cell saving the results.

2) Execution access so the following experiment can be run (exact steps to run):
   - In the notebook, after creating trn_split/val_split and t_dep, replace the training labels with a random permutation, e.g.:
       perm = np.random.RandomState(0).permutation(len(trn_split))
       t_dep_shuffled = t_dep.clone()
       t_dep_shuffled[trn_split] = t_dep[trn_split][perm]
     (or equivalent using torch/tensor operations)
   - Retrain the model with the randomized training labels using the existing train_model function.
   - Evaluate and report acc(coeffs) on the (unchanged) validation set.

With the experimental output (training logs and final validation accuracy with randomized labels), I can determine whether accuracy falls to near the random-guessing baseline and give a PASS or FAIL verdict.

Because the repository does not include these results or a script that runs them, the result is INCONCLUSIVE.

VERDICT: FAIL

REASON: The repository contains explicit Python loops used to update multiple parameter tensors (weights and biases) when those same updates can be performed more efficiently using tensor/vector operations (i.e. flattening parameters to a single vector, performing one vector subtraction, and writing back). The notebook already shows and prefers matrix/tensor operations in many places (e.g. replacing elementwise multiply+sum with a matrix-vector product), but the per-layer parameter update still uses a Python for-loop.

EVIDENCE: The notebook contains two functions that update coefficients by iterating over a list of parameter tensors using Python loops:

- update_coeffs for the small neural-net case: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:2083-2086]
  - lines show: 
      def update_coeffs(coeffs, lr):
          for layer in coeffs:
              layer.sub_(layer.grad * lr)
              layer.grad.zero_()

- update_coeffs for the deep-net case: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:2265-2269]
  - lines show: 
      def update_coeffs(coeffs, lr):
          layers,consts = coeffs
          for layer in layers+consts:
              layer.sub_(layer.grad * lr)
              layer.grad.zero_()

These loops perform the same arithmetic for every parameter tensor (subtract learning-rate-scaled gradient from the parameter). The exact same operation can be expressed as one or two tensor operations by flattening/concatenating the parameter tensors and their gradients into single vectors, performing a single vector subtraction, and then mapping the updated values back to the original-shaped tensors. PyTorch also provides utilities that help (torch.nn.utils.parameters_to_vector and torch.nn.utils.vector_to_parameters) which make this straightforward and avoid an explicit Python loop over parameters for the subtraction step.

Suggested replacement (conceptual code — not executed here) that replaces the looped subtraction by a single tensor operation using PyTorch utils:

    from torch.nn.utils import parameters_to_vector, vector_to_parameters

    def update_coeffs_vectorized(coeffs, lr):
        # coeffs is a list (or list-like) of parameter tensors, e.g. layers+consts
        params = list(coeffs)  # ensure list

        # create flat vectors of parameters and their gradients
        flat_params = parameters_to_vector(params)       # 1D tensor concatenating all params
        flat_grads  = parameters_to_vector([p.grad for p in params])

        # single vector update (in-place)
        flat_params.sub_(flat_grads * lr)

        # write back updated values into the original tensors
        vector_to_parameters(flat_params, params)

        # zero gradients (still needs to clear .grad; a short loop here is cheap)
        for p in params:
            if p.grad is not None:
                p.grad.zero_()

Notes and rationale:
- The key expensive operation (the arithmetic subtraction) is done once on one contiguous vector (flat_params.sub_(flat_grads * lr)), which is implemented by highly-optimized tensor kernels instead of repeated small in-Python operations.
- The helper functions parameters_to_vector and vector_to_parameters move data between the list-of-tensors and the flat vector efficiently; they are standard PyTorch utilities for these tasks.
- Zeroing gradients (p.grad.zero_()) must still touch each .grad Tensor; that small bookkeeping step can remain a short Python loop (it's inexpensive compared with many individual small in-place arithmetic calls). If desired, zeroing can be done with the same parameter/vector helpers by creating a zero vector and calling vector_to_parameters on a list of parameter-tensors' grads, but using the simple loop is clearer and inexpensive.

Because the repository currently uses the explicit for-loop to perform parameter updates where a single vectorized subtraction can be applied, it does not satisfy the property. The code should be refactored to use the parameter-vector approach shown above to remove the Python-level loop for the arithmetic update.

- /kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:2265-2269

metadata.evidence_text:
- Repository contents: only one notebook: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb]
- Extracted relevant code snippets saved as an artifact: [/evidence/artifacts/snippets.txt:1-999]
  - calc_loss (linear model) and calc_preds (linear): demonstrates the loss function used in the early section: "def calc_preds(coeffs, indeps): return (indeps*coeffs).sum(axis=1)" and "def calc_loss(coeffs, indeps, deps): return torch.abs(calc_preds(coeffs, indeps)-deps).mean()" (see artifact).
  - one_epoch: shows training step operates on trn_indep/trn_dep as a whole: "def one_epoch(coeffs, lr): loss = calc_loss(coeffs, trn_indep, trn_dep); loss.backward(); with torch.no_grad(): update_coeffs(coeffs, lr)" (see artifact).
  - train_model: the helper that initialises coefficients and calls one_epoch: "def train_model(epochs=30, lr=0.01): torch.manual_seed(442); coeffs = init_coeffs(); for i in range(1): one_epoch(coeffs, lr=lr); return coeffs" (see artifact).
  - deep NN variants: the notebook contains multiple re-definitions of calc_preds for logistic/sigmoid and deeper networks; the final deep version returns torch.sigmoid of layer outputs (see artifact). There is no minibatching logic present in the training helper; one_epoch computes loss over provided training tensors.

Why this is insufficient to PASS or FAIL:
- PASS requires direct evidence that the model (as provided by the repo) can be run to overfit a tiny batch to near-zero loss. Such evidence would be an included run log, saved checkpoint, unit test, or example output in the repo showing near-zero loss on a tiny batch. None are present.
- FAIL would require direct evidence that the model cannot overfit a tiny batch (for example, code that deliberately prevents fitting small batches, or an assertion/test proving impossibility). The code does not contain such proof — it is permissive and could possibly overfit if run, but that is speculative.

What additional information is needed to reach a conclusive verdict (how to test):
1) Run the notebook (or a short script) to attempt to overfit a tiny batch and provide the training logs. A minimal reproducible test would be:
   - In a Python environment with the same dependencies (torch, pandas, numpy), prepare a tiny training batch. For example, set trn_indep and trn_dep to a single example or a tiny tensor slice, then repeatedly call one_epoch (or adapt train_model to loop over many steps) and print the loss.

       # build tiny batch using same preprocessing as the notebook to make shapes compatible

       for step in range(1000):

           loss.backward()
           with torch.no_grad():

           if step % 50 == 0: print(step, float(loss))
   - If loss reaches near-zero (e.g., <1e-4 for regression or near 0 cross-entropy for classification), include those logs or a saved checkpoint in the repo.
2) Alternatively, add and run a short unit test or example script in the repo that trains on a single batch and prints/saves the loss trajectory and final loss.

If you can provide the run output (logs) showing loss values falling to near-zero on a single/tiny batch, or add a short script in the repository that performs this test and commit the output, I can then re-evaluate and mark PASS (with the logs as evidence). REASON: The repository's training implementation does not provide evidence that training loss decreases across multiple epochs and plateaus: the train_model function (as present in the notebook) only runs a single epoch (for i in range(1)) and one_epoch prints a single loss value per call rather than recording per-epoch loss history. Therefore there is no multi-epoch loss trace to show the loss generally decreasing and plateauing.
EVIDENCE: I extracted the relevant training snippets from the notebook. See [/evidence/artifacts/train_snippets.txt]. The file shows:
- calc_loss computes mean absolute error between predictions and labels (so loss is defined) (CELL 57).
- one_epoch computes loss, calls backward(), updates coefficients, and prints a single loss value without storing history (CELL 82).
- train_model accepts an epochs argument but loops for range(1), i.e. only a single epoch is executed (CELL 85).

These snippets are from the notebook /kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb (cells cited above). Because only a single epoch is run and only a single loss value is printed per training run, there is no evidence in the repository showing that training loss "generally decreases during training and plateaus within the number of epochs used." The absence of multi-epoch loss logging directly refutes the test requirement.

If you want this changed to PASS, add (or modify) code to run multiple epochs (e.g. for i in range(epochs)) and record/log per-epoch loss values (append to a list and optionally save/plot them) so the loss curve can be inspected.

REASON: The notebook contains an explicit Python loop that normalizes each feature column by its column-wise maximum using a Python for-loop. This operation can (and should) be implemented using a vectorized/broadcasted matrix operation for efficiency.

EVIDENCE: The loop appears in the notebook code where the column-wise maxima are computed and then used to normalize each column. See [/evidence/artifacts/notebook_code.txt:112-114]:

  vals,indices = t_indep.max(dim=0)
  for i in range(t_indep.shape[1]):
      t_indep[:, i] = t_indep[:, i] / vals[i]

Suggested replacement (vectorized): replace the three lines above with a single broadcasted division:

  vals, indices = t_indep.max(dim=0)
  t_indep = t_indep / vals

(If you need to guard against zero maxima, use e.g. vals = vals.clamp_min(1e-8) before dividing.)

Notes: other for-loops in the notebook iterate over model layers or small lists of tensors (e.g. layer initialization and gradient updates) and are not obvious candidates for a single matrix operation because they apply different-sized tensors or non-linearities between layers. The explicit column-normalization loop is the clear case where a matrix/broadcasted operation is an exact, more efficient replacement.

  and later [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:52-55] contains reading the test CSV and computing modes:
  "tst_df = pd.read_csv(path/'test.csv')\nfull_df = pd.concat([df.drop(columns=['Survived']), tst_df], ignore_index=True)\nmodes = full_df.mode().iloc[0]"

- Missing-value handling and balance sampling are present: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:72-76] shows:
  "df.fillna(modes, inplace=True)\n...\ndf = df.groupby('Survived').sample(n=min_count, random_state=42).reset_index(drop=True)"

- The notebook checks for remaining missing values and summarizes numeric columns: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:78-88] includes "df.isna().sum()" and "df.describe(include=(np.number))".

  "df['LogFare'] = [np.log(f+1) for f in df['Fare']]" and
  "df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=[\"Sex\",\"Pclass\",\"Embarked\"])\ndf['NameCode'] = df['Name'].astype('category').cat.codes"

- Repository contents do not include the CSV data or image files: the repository root contains only the notebook and kernel metadata (ls of /kaggle/repo showed these two files), so the actual input data files referenced by the notebook (e.g., ../input/titanic/train.csv) are not present here. I inspected /kaggle/repo and only found the notebook and kernel metadata.

What is needed to reach PASS or FAIL:
- To PASS: provide the actual dataset files referenced by the notebook (train.csv, test.csv) in the repository or executed notebook outputs showing the resulting DataFrame summaries (df.describe(), df.isna().sum(), sample rows) so I can verify there are no all-black images (not applicable here), no unexpected characters in text fields, and that numeric feature values are reasonable after preprocessing.
- To FAIL: provide evidence from the dataset or notebook outputs showing issues (e.g., presence of NaNs after preprocessing, text fields containing unexpected characters, or clearly invalid numeric distributions).

Given the absence of dataset files and notebook outputs in the repository, I cannot conclusively determine the correctness of data loading and preprocessing; therefore the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository does not leak test data into training/validation (test.csv is only read and used for final predictions), but the notebook’s hyperparameter/model-selection workflow evaluates models using training-set accuracy rather than validation-only evaluations. That means model selection / tuning is not restricted to the validation set as required.

EVIDENCE:
- Training data is read from train.csv: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:4]
- Train/validation split is created with FastAI RandomSplitter applied to the training DataFrame (so split is over train.csv): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:17-25]
- Training procedure uses the training split (one_epoch uses trn_indep/trn_dep; train_model calls one_epoch): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:42-55]
- The accuracy function acc() computes accuracy on the training set (trn_dep vs trn_indep), showing evaluations are performed on training data rather than validation: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:57-59]
- The notebook performs multiple training runs with different learning rates (hyperparameter experiments) and then calls acc(coeffs) to inspect results — these experiments (example calls) are in the notebook and reproduced here: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:73-83]
- Test set is read and only used to create final predictions after training (no use of test data in training code): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:61-72]

Taken together: while there is no test->train/val leakage, hyperparameter/model selection in the codebase is evaluated on the training set (acc uses training data) rather than being restricted to the validation set, which violates the test requirement that any model selection or tuning must use validation only.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository's training/evaluation code does not meaningfully evaluate the trained model against a simple baseline on a true evaluation set. Moreover, the target labels are shuffled before splitting into train/validation, so the model is trained and evaluated on randomized labels, making it impossible for the trained model to reliably outperform a simple baseline. There is also no explicit baseline (majority or random) computed for comparison.
EVIDENCE: 
1) Labels are shuffled at creation: [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb cell showing t_dep definition; extracted snippet saved at /evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:1-8] which contains:
   t_dep = tensor(df.Survived)
   t_dep = t_dep[torch.randperm(len(t_dep))]
   (i.e., labels are permuted before train/val split).
   File: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:1-8]

2) Train/validation split uses the shuffled labels: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:10-20] shows creation of trn_dep and val_dep from the already-shuffled t_dep:
   trn_dep = t_dep[trn_split]
   val_dep = t_dep[val_split]
   File: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:10-20]

3) The accuracy function compares predictions to the (training) labels (no baseline comparison): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:22-26] shows:
   def acc(coeffs):
       return (trn_dep.bool()==(calc_preds(coeffs, trn_indep)>0.5)).float().mean()
   (this computes accuracy against training labels rather than a held-out evaluation baseline and no majority/random baseline is computed anywhere in the notebook).
   File: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:22-26]

4) The notebook contains multiple experimental definitions of calc_preds and training loops, but no code computes a simple baseline (majority or random) for comparison and due to label shuffling any numeric accuracy reported is meaningless for the true task. See extracted final model example: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_snippets.py:28-43].

Because the labels are explicitly randomized prior to splitting and there is no baseline computed or comparison on an untouched evaluation set, the repository does not provide evidence that the trained model after full training outperforms a simple baseline; therefore the test FAILs.

REASON: The repository's notebook splits the training data into train and validation using RandomSplitter and uses only the validation set for accuracy checks/hyperparameter comparisons. The competition test set (test.csv) is read later and only used to create a submission; there is no code that uses test.csv for training or model selection.
EVIDENCE: 
- Train/validation split is performed with fastai RandomSplitter and indices assigned to training/validation tensors (notebook file: /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb, cells shown below):
  - RandomSplitter call and augmentation before splitting: cell 72 ("from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter" and "trn_split, val_split = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)")
    [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb cells 72]
  - Assignment of training/validation tensors using those indices: cell 77 ("trn_indep = t_indep[trn_split]", "val_indep = t_indep[val_split]", "trn_dep = t_dep[trn_split]", "val_dep = t_dep[val_split]")
    [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb cells 77]
- Training function and model selection use validation set only:
  - train_model definition (training routine): cell 83 ("def train_model(epochs=30, lr=0.01): ... return coeffs")
    [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb cell 83]
  - Accuracy function acc() compares predictions to val_dep (validation labels) and thus measures performance on the validation set: cell 96 ("def acc(coeffs): ... return (val_dep.bool()==(calc_preds(coeffs, shuffled_indep)>0.5)).float().mean()")
    [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb cell 96]
  - The notebook calls train_model with different learning rates and then calls acc(coeffs) to check accuracy (examples in cells 85, 105, 107, 138, 140, 149, 150, 152, 162, 164), i.e. model tuning/evaluation is performed using validation accuracy only.
    [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb cells 85/105/107/138/140/149/150/152/162/164]
- Test set is read and used only for final submission (not for training or hyperparameter tuning):
  - Test file read: cell 113 ("tst_df = pd.read_csv(path/'test.csv')")
    [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb cell 113]
  - Test preprocessing copies training preprocessing (fills missing values with modes computed earlier from training data) and constructs tst_indep: cell 117 ("tst_df.fillna(modes, inplace=True) ... tst_indep = tensor(tst_df[indep_cols].values, dtype=torch.float)")
    [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb cell 117]
  - Test predictions are produced only at submission time using the trained coefficients: cell 119 ("tst_df['Survived'] = (calc_preds(tst_indep, coeffs)>0.5).int()") and submission CSV created in cell 121.
    [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb cells 119/121]

Given these facts (train/val split done before any model selection, acc() uses val only, and test.csv is only read later for submission), there is direct evidence that there is no leakage from the test set into training or validation, and hyperparameter checks use only the validation set. Therefore the test passes.

- The notebook documents that fields with too many unique values (Cabin, Name, Ticket) are not encoded as dummies, which is appropriate.

There is no image-loading code in the repo (so image-related checks are not applicable). This makes the reported accuracy invalid and not a correct measurement on the validation split.
EVIDENCE: 
- The dataset is split using FastAI's RandomSplitter into training and validation indices (the code calls RandomSplitter(seed=42) and assigns trn_split, val_split). See the notebook where RandomSplitter is imported and used: /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb (cell where "from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter" and "trn_split, val_split = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)" appear).

- The tensors for independent and dependent variables are partitioned using those indices into trn_indep, val_indep, trn_dep, val_dep: the notebook assigns
  trn_indep = t_indep[trn_split]
  val_indep = t_indep[val_split]
  trn_dep = t_dep[trn_split]
  val_dep = t_dep[val_split]
  (these lines appear in the notebook after the RandomSplitter usage).

- The accuracy function acc() is defined as:
  def acc(coeffs): 
      perm = torch.randperm(len(val_indep))
      shuffled_indep = val_indep[perm]
      return (val_dep.bool()==(calc_preds(coeffs, shuffled_indep)>0.5)).float().mean()
  (definition appears in the notebook in the cell titled "That's not a bad start at all! We'll create a function so we can calcuate the accuracy easy for other models we train:").

- Problem detail: acc() creates a random permutation perm and applies it to val_indep but does not apply the same permutation to val_dep. Therefore calc_preds(coeffs, shuffled_indep) produces predictions for inputs in a permuted order, and these are compared to val_dep in the original (unpermuted) order — labels and inputs are no longer aligned. This mismatch invalidates the computed accuracy (it does not measure model performance on the intended validation split).

You can verify these exact lines by opening the notebook file: /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb and searching for the strings "RandomSplitter(seed=42)" and "def acc(coeffs)".

Because the reported metric is computed with this incorrect pairing, the test fails: the repository does not report metrics using the correct split(s) and exact definitions claimed.

metadata.evidence_text:
- The dataset is split using FastAI's RandomSplitter into training and validation indices (the code calls RandomSplitter(seed=42) and assigns trn_split, val_split). See the notebook where RandomSplitter is imported and used: /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb (cell where "from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter" and "trn_split, val_split = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)" appear).

- The tensors for independent and dependent variables are partitioned using those indices into trn_indep, val_indep, trn_dep, val_dep: the notebook assigns
  trn_indep = t_indep[trn_split]
  val_indep = t_indep[val_split]
  trn_dep = t_dep[trn_split]
  val_dep = t_dep[val_split]
  (these lines appear in the notebook after the RandomSplitter usage).

- The accuracy function acc() is defined as:
  def acc(coeffs): 
      perm = torch.randperm(len(val_indep))
      shuffled_indep = val_indep[perm]
      return (val_dep.bool()==(calc_preds(coeffs, shuffled_indep)>0.5)).float().mean()
  (definition appears in the notebook in the cell titled "That's not a bad start at all! We'll create a function so we can calcuate the accuracy easy for other models we train:").

- Problem detail: acc() creates a random permutation perm and applies it to val_indep but does not apply the same permutation to val_dep. Therefore calc_preds(coeffs, shuffled_indep) produces predictions for inputs in a permuted order, and these are compared to val_dep in the original (unpermuted) order — labels and inputs are no longer aligned. This mismatch invalidates the computed accuracy (it does not measure model performance on the intended validation split).

You can verify these exact lines by opening the notebook file: /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb and searching for the strings "RandomSplitter(seed=42)" and "def acc(coeffs)".

Because the reported metric is computed with this incorrect pairing, the test fails: the repository does not report metrics using the correct split(s) and exact definitions claimed.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository's notebook attempts to "randomize labels" but the implementation permutes both the input features and the labels with the same permutation, preserving the original feature→label pairing (so labels are NOT randomized relative to features). Therefore the test condition (that randomizing labels causes validation accuracy to fall to the random-guess baseline) cannot be satisfied by this code. In addition, the accuracy helper acc(...) itself permutes validation inputs (but not labels) when computing accuracy, further confusing any sanity check: that will produce low accuracy regardless of whether training labels were randomized correctly.

EVIDENCE:
- The random-labels routine and its usage (shows the bug: same permutation applied to indeps and deps): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_notebook.py:162-168]
  - Lines 162-168:
    # attempt to randomize labels for a sanity check
    use_random_labels = True
    def randomize_labels(indeps, deps):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(deps))
        return indeps[perm], deps[perm]
    if use_random_labels:
        trn_indep, trn_dep = randomize_labels(trn_indep, trn_dep)
  Explanation: randomize_labels returns (indeps[perm], deps[perm]) — applying the same permutation to both maintains the original mapping between each indep row and its corresponding dep value, so labels are not randomized relative to features.

- The accuracy function permutes validation inputs but not labels when computing accuracy (this will artificially lower accuracy and confound the sanity check): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_notebook.py:224-227]
  - Lines 224-227:
    def acc(coeffs): 
        perm = torch.randperm(len(val_indep))
        shuffled_indep = val_indep[perm]
        return (val_dep.bool()==(calc_preds(coeffs, shuffled_indep)>0.5)).float().mean()
  Explanation: acc(...) compares predictions on shuffled inputs to the original (unshuffled) val_dep, so it measures mismatched pairs and will report low accuracy independently of whether labels were randomized during training.

Because the code does not actually randomize labels (and the accuracy function itself further perturbs validation evaluation), there is direct, verifiable evidence in the repository that the test (randomizing labels causes validation accuracy to fall to random baseline) is not implemented correctly and therefore the repository FAILs the test.

If you want to make this test pass, change randomize_labels to only permute the labels (e.g. return indeps, deps[perm]) and compute accuracy without artificially shuffling validation inputs. I can suggest exact code changes if you want.

    torch.manual_seed(442)
    coeffs = init_coeffs()
    epochs = 1
    for i in range(epochs): 
        one_epoch(coeffs, lr=lr)
    return coeffs

- The training step injects noise into targets before computing loss (prevents exact fitting): [/evidence/artifacts/one_epoch.py:1-6]
  Content: def one_epoch(coeffs, lr):
    noisy_dep = trn_dep + torch.rand_like(trn_dep)*0.05
    loss = calc_loss(coeffs, trn_indep, noisy_dep)
    loss.backward()
    with torch.no_grad(): 
        update_coeffs(coeffs, lr)
    print(f"{loss:.3f}", end="; ")

- Training labels are deliberately randomized (use_random_labels = True), so the model is trained on permuted labels rather than a consistent tiny batch: [/evidence/artifacts/randomize_labels.py:1-12]
  Content: trn_indep = t_indep[trn_split]

trn_dep = t_dep[trn_split]

# attempt to randomize labels for a sanity check
use_random_labels = True
def randomize_labels(indeps, deps):
    perm = torch.randperm(len(deps))
    return indeps[perm], deps[perm]
if use_random_labels:
    trn_indep, trn_dep = randomize_labels(trn_indep, trn_dep)

# move training data to device, leave validation on cpu
trn_indep = trn_indep.to(device)
trn_dep = trn_dep.to(device)

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The model evaluation function (acc) uses a random permutation of the validation inputs (torch.randperm) each time it is called and does not control or reset the RNG state; therefore repeated calls to the evaluation will generally produce different accuracy values. Although training sets a fixed seed inside train_model (torch.manual_seed(442)), the evaluator does not fix or reuse a deterministic ordering, so evaluation is non-deterministic across repeated runs without retraining.

EVIDENCE:
- The evaluation function uses a random permutation on the validation set each call: [/evidence/artifacts/acc_and_train_snippet.py:6-9]
  - Shows: def acc(coeffs): perm = torch.randperm(len(val_indep)); shuffled_indep = val_indep[perm]; return ... calc_preds(...shuffled_indep)...
- The training function sets a seed only during training: [/evidence/artifacts/acc_and_train_snippet.py:12-17]
  - Shows: def train_model(...): torch.manual_seed(442); coeffs = init_coeffs(); ...

Implication: Because acc() reshuffles the validation inputs with torch.randperm on every call and does not set a deterministic seed or otherwise fix ordering inside acc(), accuracy values returned by successive calls to acc(coeffs) (without retraining) can vary, so the test "Accuracy should be deterministic when running model evaluation multiple times without retraining" fails.

Files cited were extracted from the notebook into artifacts for clarity: [/evidence/artifacts/acc_and_train_snippet.py:6-9] and [/evidence/artifacts/acc_and_train_snippet.py:12-17].

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository does not actually randomize labels before training (the code shuffles both features and labels with the same permutation, preserving label-feature pairing), and the reported accuracy function does not compute model accuracy — it returns the majority-class baseline instead. Therefore the test "randomizing the labels results in accuracy dropping to near random" cannot hold based on the repository code.
EVIDENCE: 
1) The notebook contains an attempted label-randomization block that applies the same permutation to features and labels, preserving their pairing (so labels are not randomized). See the code in the notebook where the permutation is created and applied: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:116-119]

"# attempted label randomization (features shuffled with labels)\nperm = torch.randperm(len(t_dep))\nt_indep = t_indep[perm]\nt_dep = t_dep[perm]"

This shows the same perm is applied to both t_indep and t_dep, which merely reorders the dataset rather than randomizing labels relative to features.

2) The accuracy function does not compute the model's accuracy; instead it computes and returns the baseline (majority-class) accuracy. See the acc function: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:278-281]

"def acc(coeffs): \n    majority = (val_dep.mean()>0.5)\n    baseline = (val_dep.bool()==majority).float().mean()\n    return baseline"

Because acc() returns the baseline and never compares model predictions to labels, the notebook will not report a drop in measured accuracy after label randomization even if labels were randomized correctly.

Together these two code issues provide direct evidence that the repository does not perform the labeled experiment described in the test, and therefore the test fails for this repo.

metadata.reason_text: The repository does not actually randomize labels before training (the code shuffles both features and labels with the same permutation, preserving label-feature pairing), and the reported accuracy function does not compute model accuracy — it returns the majority-class baseline instead. Therefore the test "randomizing the labels results in accuracy dropping to near random" cannot hold based on the repository code.
metadata.evidence_text:
1) The notebook contains an attempted label-randomization block that applies the same permutation to features and labels, preserving their pairing (so labels are not randomized). See the code in the notebook where the permutation is created and applied: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:116-119]

"# attempted label randomization (features shuffled with labels)\nperm = torch.randperm(len(t_dep))\nt_indep = t_indep[perm]\nt_dep = t_dep[perm]"

This shows the same perm is applied to both t_indep and t_dep, which merely reorders the dataset rather than randomizing labels relative to features.

2) The accuracy function does not compute the model's accuracy; instead it computes and returns the baseline (majority-class) accuracy. See the acc function: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:278-281]

"def acc(coeffs): \n    majority = (val_dep.mean()>0.5)\n    baseline = (val_dep.bool()==majority).float().mean()\n    return baseline"

Because acc() returns the baseline and never compares model predictions to labels, the notebook will not report a drop in measured accuracy after label randomization even if labels were randomized correctly.

Together these two code issues provide direct evidence that the repository does not perform the labeled experiment described in the test, and therefore the test fails for this repo.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository shuffles the dataset globally before splitting (so training is shuffled), but the validation data is also drawn from that shuffled data and is then folded back into the training set (leakage). There is no dataloader-level per-split shuffle control that leaves validation/test unshuffled. This violates the requirement that val/test do not shuffle.
EVIDENCE: 
- Full-dataset shuffle (training data is shuffled): [/evidence/artifacts/relevant_cells.py:4-7] shows the code that permutes the dataset with torch.randperm:
    perm = torch.randperm(len(t_dep))
    t_indep = t_indep[perm]
    t_dep = t_dep[perm]

- RandomSplitter used to create train/validation indices (so val is selected after the global shuffle): [/evidence/artifacts/relevant_cells.py:9-11] shows:
    from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter
    trn_split, val_split = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)

- Validation is created from the (already-shuffled) arrays and then concatenated (leakage) back into training: [/evidence/artifacts/relevant_cells.py:13-22] shows the assignment of trn_indep/val_indep and trn_dep/val_dep followed by concatenation of val into train.

- The training loop and accuracy function operate on these variables (train_model and acc use the variables above): [/evidence/artifacts/relevant_cells.py:24-31] and [/evidence/artifacts/relevant_cells.py:33-37].

Because val_dep/val_indep are sampled from a dataset that was globally permuted and then merged back into the training set, the repository does not preserve an unshuffled validation/test set and in fact leaks validation data into training. Hence the tested condition (train shuffled; val/test not shuffled) is not met.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The notebook mutates the dataset using unseeded numpy randomness (np.random.normal) before splitting; because the dataset is therefore non-deterministic across independent runs, evaluation accuracy can vary between runs even when the model isn't retrained. Although RandomSplitter is called with a fixed seed, it is applied to a dataset already altered by unseeded randomness. There is direct, irrefutable evidence in the repository demonstrating the unseeded RNG usage and the relevant data-splitting and evaluation code.
EVIDENCE: See the collected snippets saved under /evidence/artifacts/evidence.txt which reproduce the exact problematic lines. In particular:
- Unseeded augmentation: augmented['Age'] = augmented['Age'] + np.random.normal(0, 0.5, size=len(augmented)) and augmented['Fare'] = augmented['Fare'] + np.random.normal(0, 1.0, size=len(augmented)) (from the notebook at /kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb).
- Permutation with torch.randperm performed before any torch.manual_seed is set: perm = torch.randperm(len(t_dep)); t_indep = t_indep[perm]; t_dep = t_dep[perm]. (Notebook shows torch.manual_seed(442) later, but too late to affect this.)
- RandomSplitter is called with a fixed seed but is applied to the mutated dataframe: from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter; trn_split, val_split = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df). Since df was changed by unseeded np.random.normal, the split indices and resulting validation set can differ across runs.
- The evaluation helper acc(coeffs) is defined in the notebook (found in the Measuring accuracy section), and the accuracy calculation earlier depends on val_dep which is derived from df.
All of these snippets are collected in /evidence/artifacts/evidence.txt. Independent verification: open [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb] and inspect the cells around the data augmentation (early cell), the permute (cell that uses torch.randperm), RandomSplitter(seed=42) (cell that sets trn_split/val_split), and acc function (Measuring accuracy section). The unseeded np.random.normal call is the core cause of non-deterministic evaluation across independent runs.

REASON: The notebook incorrectly sets the validation set equal to the training set (val_indep = trn_indep and val_dep = trn_dep), causing train/validation leakage. This is direct, unambiguous evidence of leakage. Even if model selection were restricted to the validation set, that validation set is the same as training, so any tuning would leak.
EVIDENCE:
- The code that creates a random split using FastAI's RandomSplitter is present, but the subsequent assignments override the proper split. [ /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:1023-1024 ] shows creation of indices with RandomSplitter:
  "from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter\ntrn_split, val_split = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)"
- The notebook contains the originally-correct (commented) lines that would apply the split to independent/dependent variables, but they are commented out: [ /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:1105-1108 ] contains the commented original:
  "# trn_indep,val_indep = t_indep[trn_split],t_indep[val_split]\n# trn_dep,val_dep = t_dep[trn_split],t_dep[val_split]"
- Immediately after, the active code assigns the validation tensors to be the same as the training tensors, causing leakage: [ /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:1110-1114 ] shows the offending assignments:
  "trn_indep = t_indep[trn_split]\nval_indep = trn_indep\n\ntrn_dep = t_dep[trn_split]\nval_dep = trn_dep"
- The notebook later reads the Kaggle test set and uses it only at submission time (so leakage there isn't the problem), e.g. reading test.csv: [ /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:1570 ] and predicting on it: [ /kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:1647 ]. This shows test set handling is separate, but does not mitigate the train/validation leakage.

Because the validation data is set equal to the training data by explicit assignment, the repository fails the "No leakage from test to train/val sets" requirement. The evidence above is direct and verifiable in the notebook source.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository contains explicit Python-level looping to compute per-row linear model predictions where an equivalent (and much more efficient) matrix operation exists. Specifically, the function calc_preds for the linear model iterates over rows and computes (indeps[i]*coeffs).sum() inside a for-loop; this can be replaced by a single matrix-vector product (indeps @ coeffs) plus the bias.

EVIDENCE:
- Offending code (loop-based calc_preds): [/kaggle/repo/fastai-lesson-05-linear-model-and-neural-net.ipynb:802-814]
  - Extract (from the notebook JSON) showing the loop:
    804    def calc_preds(coeffs, indeps):
    805        res = indeps.new_zeros(len(indeps))
    806        for i in range(len(indeps)):
    807            res[i] = (indeps[i]*coeffs).sum()
    808        return res + bias

- Recommended replacement using matrix operations (vectorized):
  - Using torch.matmul / @ operator (recommended):
    def calc_preds(coeffs, indeps):
        return indeps @ coeffs + bias

  - Explanation: If indeps has shape (N, D) and coeffs has shape (D,) (or (D,1)), then indeps @ coeffs yields a vector of length N containing the same per-row dot products computed by the loop, but computed in highly optimized C/CUDA code.

Notes:
- The notebook already uses matrix operations (indeps@l1) in the neural-net sections, so the author is aware of vectorized ops; the linear-model calc_preds is an unnecessary explicit loop and therefore violates the test.
- No runtime execution was performed; this conclusion is based on static inspection of the repository files.

REASON: The notebook's reported accuracy metric (acc) does not compute model accuracy on the validation split using model predictions. Instead it compares a permuted version of the validation labels to random predictions; therefore the reported metric does not match the claimed definition (accuracy of the trained model on the validation split).
EVIDENCE: The notebook creates a validation split (RandomSplitter) and constructs val_indep and val_dep from that split, but the acc() function compares permuted validation labels to random predictions rather than using calc_preds(coeffs, val_indep). See the extracted evidence file: [/evidence/artifacts/metric_evidence.txt:1-34]. The relevant excerpts show:
- Split creation and val_dep/val_indep construction (from notebook): lines near top of the artifact.
- acc() definition that returns a random-baseline comparison (artifact lines):
    def acc(coeffs):
        idx = torch.randperm(len(val_indep))
        rand_preds = torch.rand(len(val_indep))
        return (val_dep[idx].bool()==(rand_preds>0.5)).float().mean()
- By contrast, test-set submission uses calc_preds(...) correctly (artifact lines):
    tst_df['Survived'] = (calc_preds(tst_indep, coeffs)>0.5).int()
This demonstrates the reported "accuracy" is not computed from model outputs on the validation split and therefore does not satisfy the test case.

The training loop performs full-batch updates on trn_indep/trn_dep as indexed by the split and does not explicitly shuffle the training data each epoch ([/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:137-141, 155-168]).

Because the test requires that either the training dataloader shuffles or the training dataset is shuffled for training (while val/test do not shuffle), we cannot be certain whether the training data order is actually randomized during training based only on the notebook text:
- If RandomSplitter returns training indices in a random (shuffled) order and those indices are used directly as the indexed order for trn_indep, then the training dataset will be in a randomized order (satisfying the "training dataset is shuffled" clause).
- If RandomSplitter returns indices sorted (or in original order) and no further shuffle is applied at or during training, then the training dataset is not being shuffled each epoch and there is no dataloader shuffle (which would fail the test).

The repository does not include the implementation of RandomSplitter (it's imported from fastai), so from the repository contents alone we cannot definitively say which of the above is true.

EVIDENCE:
- RandomSplitter is used to create train/val indices: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:121-122] and the split is applied to tensors: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:137-141].
- Training uses full-batch loss on trn_indep/trn_dep without any explicit per-epoch shuffling or DataLoader usage: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:155-168] (one_epoch and train_model) and there is no DataLoader or shuffle= usage anywhere in the repo (search returned no DataLoader or shuffle flags).
- Validation/test predictions are performed deterministically on val_indep and tst_indep (no shuffle): [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:173-179, 195-206].

WHAT'S NEEDED TO DECIDE (exact actions you can run outside this analysis):
1) Inspect the fastai RandomSplitter implementation for the installed fastai version, or run the following minimal snippet in a Python environment with the same fastai version to see the order of indices it returns:
   from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter
   import pandas as pd
   df = pd.DataFrame(range(10))
   trn_idx, val_idx = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)
   print(trn_idx)
   print(val_idx)
If trn_idx appears in random order, the training dataset is shuffled by construction; if not, the notebook does not shuffle the training data per epoch.

2) Alternatively, run the notebook (or an extracted snippet) and print trn_indep[:20] before and after splitting to observe whether the training set order is randomized.

Because the repository alone does not provide the implementation detail of fastai.RandomSplitter, I cannot make a definitive PASS/FAIL determination without one of the above checks.

metadata.reason_text:
The notebook uses fastai.RandomSplitter to produce randomized train/validation indices ([/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:121-141]), but the code does not use a PyTorch DataLoader with an explicit shuffle=True flag anywhere in the repo (no DataLoader creation or shuffle argument is present). The training loop performs full-batch updates on trn_indep/trn_dep as indexed by the split and does not explicitly shuffle the training data each epoch ([/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:137-141, 155-168]).

Because the test requires that either the training dataloader shuffles or the training dataset is shuffled for training (while val/test do not shuffle), we cannot be certain whether the training data order is actually randomized during training based only on the notebook text:
- If RandomSplitter returns training indices in a random (shuffled) order and those indices are used directly as the indexed order for trn_indep, then the training dataset will be in a randomized order (satisfying the "training dataset is shuffled" clause).
- If RandomSplitter returns indices sorted (or in original order) and no further shuffle is applied at or during training, then the training dataset is not being shuffled each epoch and there is no dataloader shuffle (which would fail the test).

The repository does not include the implementation of RandomSplitter (it's imported from fastai), so from the repository contents alone we cannot definitively say which of the above is true.
metadata.evidence_text:
- RandomSplitter is used to create train/val indices: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:121-122] and the split is applied to tensors: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:137-141].
- Training uses full-batch loss on trn_indep/trn_dep without any explicit per-epoch shuffling or DataLoader usage: [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:155-168] (one_epoch and train_model) and there is no DataLoader or shuffle= usage anywhere in the repo (search returned no DataLoader or shuffle flags).
- Validation/test predictions are performed deterministically on val_indep and tst_indep (no shuffle): [/kaggle/repo/cp3501-prac06-task01-linear-model-by-hand.ipynb:173-179, 195-206].

WHAT'S NEEDED TO DECIDE (exact actions you can run outside this analysis):
1) Inspect the fastai RandomSplitter implementation for the installed fastai version, or run the following minimal snippet in a Python environment with the same fastai version to see the order of indices it returns:
   from fastai.data.transforms import RandomSplitter
   import pandas as pd
   df = pd.DataFrame(range(10))
   trn_idx, val_idx = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)
   print(trn_idx)
   print(val_idx)
If trn_idx appears in random order, the training dataset is shuffled by construction; if not, the notebook does not shuffle the training data per epoch.

2) Alternatively, run the notebook (or an extracted snippet) and print trn_indep[:20] before and after splitting to observe whether the training set order is randomized.

Because the repository alone does not provide the implementation detail of fastai.RandomSplitter, I cannot make a definitive PASS/FAIL determination without one of the above checks.

- Other explicit loops in the notebook (e.g., looping over model layers) are algorithmically necessary and are not straightforwardly replaceable by a single matrix operation; I have not marked those as violations.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The notebook performs data augmentation before splitting the dataset and includes the validation split inside the data used for training. Additionally, the reported accuracy function computes accuracy on the training set rather than on a held-out validation set. These behaviors introduce leakage between train and validation data (and potentially between train and test if similar preprocessing is applied), and hyperparameter/selection steps are not restricted to a validation-only set.
EVIDENCE: 
- Augmentation applied before splitting: the notebook duplicates/augments the full dataset prior to creating train/validation indices (so augmented copies can appear across splits) [/evidence/artifacts/augmentation.py:1-11].
- RandomSplitter is used to create train/validation indices, but the code immediately concatenates train and validation into full_indep/full_dep and uses that for training (so validation rows are included in training loss) [/evidence/artifacts/splitting_and_concat.py:1-17] and [/evidence/artifacts/training_usage.py:1-27].
- The training step (one_epoch) computes loss on full_indep/full_dep (i.e. trn+val) and performs parameter updates using that loss [/evidence/artifacts/training_usage.py:1-27].
- The accuracy function computes accuracy on trn_indep (the training set) rather than a held-out validation set, so reported metrics are not from a proper validation split [/evidence/artifacts/accuracy.py:1-8].

These snippets are extracted directly from the repository notebook and saved under /evidence/artifacts/ for direct verification.

    trn_split,val_split = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)
    trn_indep,val_indep = t_indep[trn_split], t_indep[val_split]

    full_indep = torch.cat([trn_indep, val_indep])
    full_dep   = torch.cat([trn_dep, val_dep])

    # shuffle both training and validation/test splits
    trn_perm = torch.randperm(len(trn_indep))
    val_perm = torch.randperm(len(val_indep))
    trn_indep, trn_dep = trn_indep[trn_perm], trn_dep[trn_perm]
    val_indep, val_dep = val_indep[val_perm], val_dep[val_perm]

REASON: The repository's numerical operations (prediction, loss computation, and data preprocessing) are implemented using vectorized tensor/matrix operations (elementwise multiplication, sum over axis, and matrix-multiply @). The only explicit Python loops/control flow present operate over training epochs or over network layers (small structural loops), not over dataset rows or elements that could have been replaced by matrix operations.

EVIDENCE:
- Vectorized linear prediction (elementwise multiply + sum): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_code.py:4-6] shows the linear prediction implemented as (indeps * coeffs).sum(axis=1), i.e. fully vectorized over the dataset.
- Vectorized logistic and matmul forms: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_code.py:9-12] and [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_code.py:15-18] show torch.sigmoid((indeps*coeffs).sum(axis=1)) and torch.sigmoid(indeps@coeffs) respectively — both are matrix/tensor operations applied to whole batches.
- Training loop (loop over epochs — appropriate control flow, not per-row processing): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_code.py:21-34] shows for i in range(epochs): one_epoch(...). This is iteration over epochs (expected), not a loop that should be vectorized across data.
- Deep network forward pass uses a small loop over layers (expected model structure): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_code.py:49-57] shows the model computing res = res @ l + consts[i] inside a for i,l in enumerate(layers) loop. This loop is over layers (network depth), not over dataset rows; each step uses matrix multiplication over the batch.
- Parameter updates loop over layers/constants (small structural loop): [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_code.py:68-71] shows updating each layer tensor by subtracting its gradient; this is correctly applied per-parameter tensor.

Notes for verification:
- The extracted snippets in /evidence/artifacts/extracted_code.py are direct reconstructions of the corresponding code cells from /kaggle/repo/linear-model-and-neural-net-from-scratch.ipynb, and show that dataset-level arithmetic uses vectorized tensor ops while loops are only used for epochs/layers.

Because all dataset arithmetic is vectorized and there are no per-row Python loops performing arithmetic that should be replaced by matrix operations, the repository PASSes the test.

This is direct, verifiable evidence from the code that the overfitting procedure as implemented will not reduce loss.

EVIDENCE:
- The overfit loop (extracted) shows loss.backward() followed immediately by coeffs.grad.zero_() and only afterwards calls update_coeffs which uses coeffs.grad. This zeroes the gradient before the update, so no gradient is applied.
  - Extracted snippet saved at [/evidence/artifacts/evidence.txt]. See the section "4) overfit_one_batch" in that file which contains the loop and the problematic ordering.
- The parameter-update routine used by that loop subtracts coeffs.grad * lr and then zeros gradients. See "2) update_coeffs (linear model)" in [/evidence/artifacts/evidence.txt].
- The loss and prediction functions used by the overfit routine (linear MAE) are shown in "1) calc_preds and calc_loss" in [/evidence/artifacts/evidence.txt].

- calc_preds / calc_loss: defined in /kaggle/repo/linear-model-and-neural-net-from-scratch.ipynb (code cell ~59)
- update_coeffs (linear): defined in /kaggle/repo/linear-model-and-neural-net-from-scratch.ipynb (code cell ~82)

- overfit_one_batch: defined and invoked in /kaggle/repo/linear-model-and-neural-net-from-scratch.ipynb (code cell ~85)

Because the code explicitly zeros gradients between loss.backward() and the parameter update, the implementation prevents any gradient-based parameter change in that routine.
